newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bavarian leader names conditions for Czech accord.
newsitem.headline: Bavarian leader names conditions for Czech accord.

text.p: The premier of the German state of Bavaria, a key player in German-Czech relations, said on Thursday a planned declaration of post-war reconciliation would not be signed until Prague talked to expelled ethnic Germans.

Bavaria has made itself the advocate of the survivors or decendants of 2.5 million "Sudeten Germans" expelled in the mid- 1940s after they were collectively held responsible for betraying Czechoslovakia during the 1938-45 Nazi occupation.

Bonn and Prague have been negotiating in secret for more than a year but have still not managed to approve the text, intended symbolically to set aside resentment which lingers between the two neighbours as a result of the war.
Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber told German Radio that a signing before the end of the year "depends on whether the text is acceptable for those who are seriously affected".
"And that depends on whether...there is readiness from anyone on the Czech side to have talks with the Sudeten Germans," he said.
More than a million Sudeten Germans in Bavaria make up an important constituency for Stoiber's Christian Social Union, a member of the ruling coalition in Bonn.
Prague has always insisted that international relations are a matter for governments and that it will deal only with Bonn.
Stoiber did not specify who the Sudeten Germans would accept as a partner for discussions, but said "their offer to speak to any agency at all on the Czech side has never been taken up".
He added that "it must be possible for the Czech side now to say, without any material claims arising, that the expulsion (of the ethnic Germans) was wrong under international law".
In a newspaper interview published on Wednesday, Czech President Vaclav Havel suggested that a draft text had already been agreed by negotiators on both sides.
"Now it's a question of mobilising enough political will to accept the text. It seems to me that the hold-up is more on the German side than the Czech side," he told the Sueddeutsche Zeitung.
